newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU states seek major dairy reform.
newsitem.headline: EU states seek major dairy reform.

text.p: Six EU states, enough to force the issue, sought major changes to the European Union's complex system of milk production quotas on Monday.
Sweden, Britain, Denmark, Italy, Spain and Greece were for different reasons seeking either to dismantle or change the system introduced in 1984 to stabilise the market.

"There's a blocking minority against continuation of the present system," EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler told reporters on the second day of an informal meeting of EU farm ministers in the southern Dutch town of Middelburg.
Speaking during a visit to the massive Scheldt sea defence barrier, he said some northern member states wanted a freer system while southern countries were demanding higher quotas.
"The system does not function very well for either producers or consumers. It's very complicated," Swedish Farm Minister Annika Ahnberg told Reuters.
Britain agreed. It wants to reduce prices to world levels over five years and to relax production controls to allow farmers in different member states to transfer quotas.
"We don't think the present system is sustainable," British Farm Minister Jack Cunningham told Reuters.
He said pressure from the World Trade Organisation, the EU's expansion eastwards and internal problems would force changes.
Denmark wants reforms to be able to compete for Asian markets against New Zealand, Australia and the United States.
"We want something done quickly," said Danish Farm Minister Henrik Dam Kristensen, adding that Denmark wants also to export partly without subsidies. France also backs this view.
Spain, Italy and Greece want to be allowed to produce more milk to satisfy domestic demand.
Spanish Farm Minister Loyola de Palacio said Spanish milk output was cut by 1.5 million tonnes after it joined the EU and its quota only covered 75 percent of Spanish needs.
"It creates problems for our producers. We import cheese and other processed products from EU countries. Consumption is increasing," she said.
Spain had been heavily penalised for exceeding its quota, de Palacio said, noting that other countries produced surpluses that were exported with the help of EU subsidies.
Italy, where angry milk producers blocked roads earlier this year, has demanded a 600,000 tonnes increase in its quota to 10.5 million tonnes.
But in the longer term it wants to get rid of quotas and compensate farmers for any losses due to lower prices.
"We want a progressive dismantling of the quota system over six years," said Italian Farm Minister Michele Pinto.

But a majority of countries, led by Germany, wants to extend the quota system when it expires at the end of March 2000. They say it has stabilised prices at profitable levels and helped to keep thousands of small farmers in poor areas in business.
